z-m-40-01.title: Let's choose a domain so that an inverse function exists
z-m-40-01.topic: One-to-one correspondence and inverse functions: shrinking the domain to an interval so that f(x)=x²−2x has an inverse function
z-m-40-01.goal: Understand that a table checking a few values is not evidence for “one-to-one,” design an interval yourself for the domain of a quadratic function so that the same value does not occur twice, and then confirm that the domain of the inverse function is the range of the original function.
z-m-40-01.material: Consider the function f(x) = x² − 2x (read as: 'x squared minus 2x'). The domain has not been chosen yet. Saying that f has an inverse function on some set means that no two different x in that set give the same value of f (then the range of f becomes the domain of the inverse function). Seojin made a table where f(x) was −1, 0, 3, 8 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4, all different, and said, “f has an inverse function on all real numbers.”
z-m-40-01.thinking.0: Considering how far sample evidence reaches
z-m-40-01.thinking.1: Designing several domains that satisfy the condition
z-m-40-01.thinking.2: Judging how being one-to-one changes depending on the condition on the domain
z-m-40-01.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you have already learned one-to-one correspondence and the meaning of inverse functions (the correspondence that swaps domain and range).
z-m-40-01.prereq.1: Experience calculating function values of a quadratic function and sketching the rough shape of a parabola
z-m-40-01.s.s1.prompt: Can Seojin's table be evidence for the statement “f has an inverse function on all real numbers”? Choose what can be said from the table.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.hint.0: Pick an x that is not in the table, calculate the value of f, and compare whether it overlaps with the values in the table.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put in a few values not in the table, such as x = 0, −1, 5, and see whether a value that already appeared comes up again.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.o.a: The four values in the table are all different, so even if the domain is all real numbers, we can say the same value does not appear twice
z-m-40-01.s.s1.r.a: This thinking stretches a few checked results to all the x that have not been looked at yet. Test x values outside the table too.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.o.b: As x increased, f(x) also increased, so f is an increasing function, and therefore one-to-one
z-m-40-01.s.s1.r.b: This thinking stretches the increasing trend seen in the table to the whole interval. Check whether the same trend holds on the side where x is less than 1.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.o.c: The table covers only x = 1 to 4, so whether the same value appears at an x outside the table has to be checked separately
z-m-40-01.s.s1.r.c: This thinking examines how far the evidence reaches in terms of x.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.o.d: If we check ten more integers and they are all different, we can conclude it is one-to-one on all real numbers
z-m-40-01.s.s1.r.d: This thinking holds that increasing the number of checked points settles the whole. Checking a finite number of points, however many, cannot rule out a counterexample.
z-m-40-01.s.s1.explain: The table shows only that the same value does not appear at x = 1, 2, 3, 4. We cannot know about x outside the table, and in fact there are x with the same value, such as f(0) = 0 = f(2). Checking a finite number of points does not settle that the whole is one-to-one.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.prompt: Build 3 domains [a, b] that include x = 0 and for which an inverse function exists. Conditions: a and b are integers, −6 ≤ a < b ≤ 6, and the length of the interval b − a is 2 or more.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.hint.0: Sketch the graph of f(x) = x² − 2x roughly and look at where the two points at the same height are.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.hint.1: Find the other x that has the same value as x = 0, and think about the condition for that point not to be inside the interval.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.var.a: Left end a of the interval
z-m-40-01.s.s2.var.b: Right end b of the interval
z-m-40-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer with a < b.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be an integer less than b.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.ok.c2: You kept the range and length conditions.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Both −6 ≤ a, b ≤ 6 and b − a ≥ 2 must hold.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The interval must include x = 0 (a ≤ 0 ≤ b).
z-m-40-01.s.s2.ok.c4: Inside this interval there are no two different points with the same f value.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Inside this interval there are two different points with the same f value. Find a pair of points at the same height inside the interval.
z-m-40-01.s.s2.explain: Since f(x) = (x − 1)² − 1, the graph is symmetric left and right about the axis x = 1. If the interval spans both sides of x = 1, two points at the same distance from the axis have the same value (for example, in [0, 2], f(0) = f(2) = 0). To include x = 0 and avoid this, we need b ≤ 1, and then f keeps decreasing on the interval.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.prompt: Seojin chose the domain [−2, 0]. On this interval, which is the domain of the inverse function f⁻¹ of f (= the range of f)?
z-m-40-01.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate f(−2), f(−1), f(0) and look at how the values change on the interval.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.hint.1: Check with one more point whether the values at the two ends of the interval become the two ends of the range.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.r.a: This thinking treats the domain of the inverse function and the domain of the original function as the same set. In an inverse function, the places of input and output are swapped.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.r.b: This thinking checks the function values f(0) = 0 and f(−2) = 8 at the two ends of the interval and connects what is between them.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.r.c: This thinking uses the value −1 at the vertex as the minimum regardless of the interval. Check whether the vertex is inside this interval.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.r.d: This thinking leaves the upper end open without checking it. Calculate the value at the left end of the interval, x = −2.
z-m-40-01.s.s3.explain: f(−2) = 8, f(−1) = 3, f(0) = 0, so on this interval f decreases and takes every value from 0 to 8. So the domain of f⁻¹ is 0 ≤ x ≤ 8.

z-m-40-02.title: In the solution that wrote the inverse function, which is the first line that goes wrong?
z-m-40-02.topic: Inverse functions: the formula of the inverse of a quadratic function with a restricted domain, and checking a solution
z-m-40-02.goal: Find the first line that goes wrong in an inverse function solution, explain the correct formula and why that sign was chosen (the domain condition), and check the inverse function by sending function values back.
z-m-40-02.material: We want to find the inverse function g of the function f(x) = x² − 4x + 1 (domain: x ≥ 2). Below is Haeun's solution. (The square root symbol √ is read as 'root'. √(x + 3) is read as 'root of x plus 3'.)
z-m-40-02.thinking.0: Finding the error line by line in a solution
z-m-40-02.thinking.1: Choosing a way to check that the inverse function is correct
z-m-40-02.thinking.2: Justifying the sign of the square root by the domain condition
z-m-40-02.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you have already learned the meaning of inverse functions and of the square root symbol.
z-m-40-02.prereq.1: Knowing that a quadratic expression can be written in the form (x − p)² + q (textbook quadratic function level)
z-m-40-02.prereq.2: The relation that if f(x) = y, then for the inverse function g of f, g(y) = x
z-m-40-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Haeun's solution that goes wrong.
z-m-40-02.s.s1.hint.0: Compare, one line at a time, how the expression in the line right before changed in each line.
z-m-40-02.s.s1.hint.1: In the formula y − 2 = √(x + 3) in line 3, try for yourself what you have to do to leave only y.
z-m-40-02.s.s1.line.0: Swapping x and y gives x = y² − 4y + 1, and here y ≥ 2.
z-m-40-02.s.s1.line.2: From y ≥ 2, we have y − 2 ≥ 0, so y − 2 = √(x + 3).
z-m-40-02.s.s1.line.4: So the inverse function of f is g(x) = √(x + 3) − 2.
z-m-40-02.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 4. In y − 2 = √(x + 3), moving −2 to the right side makes it +2, so it should be y = 2 + √(x + 3). Line 5 carries over this mistake as it is. Lines 1 to 3 are correct.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.prompt: We want to test whether g(x) = √(x + 3) − 2 that Haeun found is really the inverse function of f. Which test shows the problem most directly?
z-m-40-02.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute one value of x (for example 3) into the formula of f and find y first.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute that y into Haeun's g and calculate whether the original x comes out, and compare.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.o.a: Find g(3), then compare whether that value is the same as f(3)
z-m-40-02.s.s2.r.a: This thinking treats the inverse function as a function that gives the same values as f. An inverse function takes the output of f as its input.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.o.b: Check whether the graph of g is drawn for x ≥ −3
z-m-40-02.s.s2.r.b: This thinking looks at the domain but cannot see whether the formula is right. Whether a formula is right or wrong shows up only by testing with function values.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.o.c: Set up and solve the equation to see whether there is an x with f(x) = g(x)
z-m-40-02.s.s2.r.c: This thinking treats the points where f and g meet as evidence of an inverse function. The meeting points are not directly related to the inverse relation.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.o.d: Find f(3), then put that value into g and see whether 3 comes out
z-m-40-02.s.s2.r.d: This thinking tries to test with values the fact that inverse functions undo each other.
z-m-40-02.s.s2.explain: For the inverse function g, if f(x) = y, then g(y) = x must hold. f(3) = −2, but g(−2) = √1 − 2 = −1, which is not 3. With the correct g(x) = 2 + √(x + 3), g(−2) = 2 + 1 = 3.
z-m-40-02.s.s3.prompt: Write the corrected solution in one or two sentences. Include the correct g(x) and the reason the value of the square root was chosen on the positive side in line 3 (relate it to the fact that the domain of f is x ≥ 2).
z-m-40-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write which part of the formula changed at the moment the sign was changed.
z-m-40-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how the original domain x ≥ 2 turns into the range of values of the inverse function.
z-m-40-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The correct inverse function is ..., and since ..., ...
z-m-40-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that if you put the output of f (for example f(3) = −2) into the formula you wrote, the original input comes back?
z-m-40-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect “the reason for choosing + for the square root” with the domain condition?
z-m-40-02.s.s3.model.0: The correct inverse function is g(x) = 2 + √(x+3). Since y ≥ 2, y − 2 ≥ 0, so we take the positive value of the square root, and when moving −2 over, it becomes +2.
z-m-40-02.s.s3.model.1: g(x) = √(x+3) + 2 is correct. The original domain is x ≥ 2, so the values of the inverse function must also be 2 or more, so −√ is not allowed, and I also checked that f(3) = −2 and g(−2) = 3 bring us back.
z-m-40-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that includes the check.

z-m-40-03.title: If the formulas look the same, are the graphs the same too?
z-m-40-03.topic: Rewriting rational functions and their domains: comparing the graphs of (x²−1)/(x−1) and x+1
z-m-40-03.goal: Understand that for two expressions that look the same after simplifying to be called the same function, their domains must also be the same, and state by cases when it is fine to draw them as the same graph and when it is not.
z-m-40-03.material: There are two functions f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) and g(x) = x + 1. (Read as: 'x squared minus 1, divided by x minus 1'.) Unless a domain is written separately, we take it to be all real numbers for which the expression can be calculated. Jia said, “The numerator x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), and if you cancel, it becomes x + 1, so f and g are the same function and their graphs are the same.”
z-m-40-03.thinking.0: Choosing the first thing to check to test the claim
z-m-40-03.thinking.1: Telling apart evidence for sameness and evidence for difference
z-m-40-03.thinking.2: Saying that the answer changes depending on the condition
z-m-40-03.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know factoring, canceling fractional expressions, and the convention that the domain of a function is all real numbers for which the expression can be calculated.
z-m-40-03.prereq.1: The fact that if the denominator is 0, the value of the expression is not defined
z-m-40-03.prereq.2: The graph of the linear function y = x + 1 (a straight line)
z-m-40-03.s.s1.prompt: We want to test Jia's claim. Choose what should be checked first.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute x = 1 into the formula of f. What happens?
z-m-40-03.s.s1.hint.1: Also substitute x = 1 into the formula of g, and compare the two results.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.o.a: See whether the ranges of x for which the two expressions can be calculated are the same
z-m-40-03.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that recalls that saying functions are the same also includes the domain.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.o.b: See whether the values of the two expressions are the same at x = 2, 3, 4
z-m-40-03.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that tries to decide the functions are the same from a few points where the values are equal. They can differ at x values that were not tested.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.o.c: See whether the graph is a straight line, since both expressions are linear
z-m-40-03.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that assumes f is already a simplified linear expression. The formula of f is in fraction form.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.o.d: Rewrite g(x) in fraction form to give it the same shape as f
z-m-40-03.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that treats functions as the same once the shapes of the formulas match. Changing the shape can change the range of x for which it can be calculated.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.explain: For two functions to be the same, both the domain and the correspondence must be the same. So the most direct check is first to compare the range of x for which each expression can be calculated.
z-m-40-03.s.s1.acc.0: Calculating a few values is a good start. However, the fact that they are equal at x = 2, 3, 4 cannot catch a difference at an untested value such as x = 1.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the grounds that can be used to show that f and g are not the same function.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.hint.0: Look at each choice one by one, separating whether it shows “difference” or shows only the “same” side.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare what happens when you substitute x = 1 into f and g with the choices.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.o.a: At x = 1, g(1) = 2, but f(1) is not defined because the denominator is 0
z-m-40-03.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that the fact that only one side has a value at one point shows the difference between the two functions.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.o.b: At x = 2, f(2) = 3 and g(2) = 3, so the two functions have the same value
z-m-40-03.s.s2.r.b: The fact that the values are equal at one point is neither evidence that the functions are the same nor evidence that they are different.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.o.c: The domain of f is the real numbers with x ≠ 1, and the domain of g is all real numbers
z-m-40-03.s.s2.r.c: This is thinking that uses the criterion that functions with different domains are not the same function.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.o.d: For every x with x ≠ 1, f(x) = x + 1 holds, so the values of the two expressions are equal
z-m-40-03.s.s2.r.d: Being equal for x ≠ 1 is only evidence on the “same” side, and it says nothing about the difference at x = 1.
z-m-40-03.s.s2.explain: At x = 1, f has no value and g is 2, and also the domains are different, so the two functions are not the same. The facts that the values are equal at x = 2 or that the expressions are equal for x ≠ 1 are evidence for the “same” side, so they cannot show a difference.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to Jia. Explain by separating the cases where f and g may be drawn as the same graph and the cases where they may not, including what is different on the graph.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence what happens in the two expressions when you substitute x = 1.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how things would change in a situation where x can never be 1.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Jia, the two expressions are ... when ..., but ...
z-m-40-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write in your own words the condition of the situation where it is okay to say they are the same?
z-m-40-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the “not okay” case, did you point out specifically which point on the graph is different?
z-m-40-03.s.s3.model.0: As long as x is not 1, the two expressions give the same value, so if we deal only with places where x ≠ 1, we can draw them as the same graph. But f is not defined at x = 1, so the graph of f is the line y = x + 1 with the single point (1, 2) missing.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.model.1: We can't say they are the same function. When x is 1, f has no value because the denominator is 0, but g is 2. So the graphs overlap except at 1, but f has a hole. If the problem deals only with the range x > 1, the results are the same even if we swap them.
z-m-40-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer that mentions the hole directly.

z-m-40-04.title: On a round trip, how fast must the return trip be for the average speed?
z-m-40-04.topic: Average speed of a round trip expressed with a rational function: how it changes with the speed on the way back, and its limit
z-m-40-04.goal: Check with times that the average speed of a round trip is not the arithmetic mean of the speeds, look at the limit on the average even if the return speed is raised through prediction and calculation, and then find the speeds that satisfy a condition yourself.
z-m-40-04.material: A bus makes a round trip on the same road. On the way there it runs at a constant speed of 30 km per hour, and on the way back it runs at a constant speed of x km per hour. The one-way distance D km is not known, and there are no stops along the way. Average speed is defined as (total distance traveled) ÷ (total time taken).
z-m-40-04.thinking.0: Revising an intuitive prediction with new information
z-m-40-04.thinking.1: Reading the shape of the change (large at first, then smaller and smaller)
z-m-40-04.thinking.2: Finding several values that satisfy a condition
z-m-40-04.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know speed = distance ÷ time and how to calculate with fractional expressions.
z-m-40-04.prereq.1: Calculating with rational (fractional) expressions, and the sense that a fraction gets smaller as its denominator gets larger
z-m-40-04.prereq.2: The convention that average speed = total distance ÷ total time taken
z-m-40-04.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what the round-trip average speed would be.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.hint.0: Fix the one-way distance at a specific value such as 60 km, and find the time taken on the way there and on the way back separately.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.hint.1: After finding the round-trip distance and the total time taken, test whether the result changes when you change the one-way distance to another value.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Take the day when the speed on the way back is 60 km per hour as an example. The one-way distance D is not known yet.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What would the round-trip average speed be on this day?
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If D = 60 km, the way there takes 60 ÷ 30 = 2 hours and the way back takes 60 ÷ 60 = 1 hour, so a round trip of 120 km took 3 hours. The average speed is 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h. The same result comes out for other values of D (D cancels). It is less than 45 because more time was spent running at the slower speed.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is thinking that takes the arithmetic mean of the speeds (the middle of 30 and 60) as the average speed.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is thinking that takes into account that more time was spent running at the slower speed.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is thinking that the faster part has a greater effect. Compare the time taken on each part.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We don't know D, so we can't know the average speed either
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is thinking that you can calculate only if the distance is specific. Try setting D to 60 and compare with other values.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Look at the day when the speed on the way back was raised to 120 km per hour.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: The speed on the way back has doubled (60 → 120). How will the average speed change from 40 km/h?
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If D = 120 km, the way there takes 4 hours and the way back takes 1 hour, so the total is 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km/h. Even though the speed was doubled, the average increased by only 20%. This is because the time taken on the way there stays the same, so the total time does not drop to half.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It increases to nearly double, close to 80 km/h
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is thinking that if the speed on the way back doubles, the average also doubles in proportion.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The average speed hardly changes and stays near 40
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is thinking that the change in the speed on the way back hardly affects the average.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It increases from 40 but falls short of doubling
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is thinking that takes into account that the time taken on the way there stays the same.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It becomes 30 km/h, the same as the speed on the way there
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is thinking that the fast part cancels out in the average.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Even if the speed on the way back is raised to 300 km per hour, the average speed is about 54.5 km/h.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Assuming the speed on the way back can be made as large as you like, is it possible for the round-trip average speed to reach 60 km per hour?
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The average speed is 60x ÷ (30 + x). The time on the way there is already used up, so even if the time on the way back is made close to 0, the average only gets close to 2D ÷ (D/30) = 60 and does not reach it. If x = 150 it is 50, if 300 it is about 54.5, and if 600 it is about 57.1.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: If you run fast enough on the way back, you can eventually reach it
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is thinking that if you raise the speed, the average also rises without limit.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: If the speed on the way back is 90 km per hour, it becomes exactly 60
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is thinking that it fits exactly at a particular speed. Calculate for yourself the average when the speed is 90 km per hour.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: A moment comes when it reaches 60; it is just not realistic
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is thinking that treats the limit value as a value that can be reached. Work out how much time it would have to take for the average to be 60.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It can't be reached. It only gets close to 60
z-m-40-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is thinking that takes into account that the time taken on the way there is already fixed.
z-m-40-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you may have thought of the average speed as the average of the speeds (45). What information (the time taken) changed that thinking? Explain the shape in which the average increases as you raise the speed on the way back (large at first, then smaller and smaller) and why a limit of 60 appears.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose the speed x on the way back (km per hour) so that the round-trip average speed is from 50 km per hour to 55 km per hour, and find 3 different values of x. x is a positive integer, and the speed on the way there is 30 km per hour.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.hint.0: Fix the one-way distance at one value, put values in for the speed x on the way back, and calculate the average speed.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.hint.1: Change x to 100, 200, 300 and so on, and narrow down toward where the average speed falls between 50 and 55.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.var.x: Speed x on the way back (km/h)
z-m-40-04.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be an integer greater than 0.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The average speed is 50 or more.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The average speed is less than 50. Recalculate the average from the times taken on the way there and on the way back.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The average speed is 55 or less.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The average speed is greater than 55. Recalculate the average.
z-m-40-04.s.s2.explain: The average speed is 60x ÷ (30 + x), and the values of x for which it is from 50 to 55 are from 150 to 330. As x gets larger, the average increases but levels off near 60, so the range of allowed x is wide.

z-m-40-05.title: A radical function whose endpoint is (−2, 1): is there only one formula?
z-m-40-05.topic: The radical function y=√(ax+b)+c: the freedom that remains when the formula is fixed by endpoint information
z-m-40-05.goal: Judge how many constants of a radical function the information about one endpoint determines and how many it leaves, build different formulas that satisfy the condition yourself, and explain what more is needed to determine the curve uniquely.
z-m-40-05.material: On the classroom screen, the graph of the radical function y = √(ax + b) + c (read as: 'square root of a x plus b, plus c') appeared. The curve has its left endpoint at (−2, 1) and extends from there toward the upper right. a, b, c are constants, and since it extends to the right, a > 0. It is not known which other points the curve passes through.
z-m-40-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
z-m-40-05.thinking.1: Designing different formulas that satisfy the condition
z-m-40-05.thinking.2: Saying what additional information is needed
z-m-40-05.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know that the graph of the radical function y = √(ax + b) + c starts at an endpoint and extends to one side.
z-m-40-05.prereq.1: Numbers whose square root is an integer (perfect squares)
z-m-40-05.prereq.2: The calculation of finding the value of y by substituting x = k into the formula
z-m-40-05.s.s1.prompt: Is it possible that a, b, c are all determined uniquely by only the information that the endpoint is (−2, 1)?
z-m-40-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what the value inside the root must be when you substitute the x-coordinate of the endpoint, −2, into the formula √(ax + b) + c.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.hint.1: Build two formulas with the same endpoint but different a, and compare whether the graphs are the same.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.o.a: It is determined: from the coordinates of the endpoint, b = −2, c = 1, and a = 1
z-m-40-05.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that moves the coordinates of the endpoint into the constants as they are. If you substitute x = −2 into the formula, you can check the meaning of the endpoint.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.o.b: c is determined but a remains, and b is determined by a
z-m-40-05.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that examines how the information of the endpoint connects to how many constants.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.o.c: It is not determined: a, b, c can each be chosen freely
z-m-40-05.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that one point gives no restriction at all among the constants. Write down the condition the endpoint gives to the formula.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.o.d: It is determined: it passes through the endpoint, so all three constants are determined uniquely
z-m-40-05.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that one condition determines all three constants. Build two formulas with the same endpoint and compare them.
z-m-40-05.s.s1.explain: The y-coordinate of the endpoint is c, so c = 1. At the endpoint the value inside the root is 0, so −2a + b = 0, that is, b = 2a. a is still free, so every formula of the form y = √(a(x + 2)) + 1 is a candidate. For example, if a = 1 then y = √(x + 2) + 1, and if a = 4 then y = √(4x + 8) + 1.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.prompt: Among y = √(ax + b) + c with endpoint (−2, 1) and extending to the right, build 3 formulas with different a for which the value of y at x = −1 is an integer. a, b, c are integers and a ≤ 20.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what the value inside the root must be at the endpoint, and substitute the coordinates of the endpoint into the formula.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what number must be left inside the root when you substitute x = −1 for the square root to be an integer.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.var.a: a (coefficient of x inside the root)
z-m-40-05.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, c are integers and 0 < a ≤ 20.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers and 0 < a ≤ 20.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The y-coordinate of the endpoint is 1.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.fail.c2: You have to choose the constants so that the y-coordinate of the endpoint is 1.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.ok.c3: At x = −2 the value inside the root is 0.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.fail.c3: At x = −2 the value inside the root is not 0. Adjust it so that the endpoint is (−2, 1).
z-m-40-05.s.s2.ok.c4: At x = −1 the value of y is an integer.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.fail.c4: At x = −1 the value of y is not an integer.
z-m-40-05.s.s2.explain: From the endpoint condition, b = 2a and c = 1, so y = √(a(x + 2)) + 1. When x = −1, y = √a + 1, so it is an integer only when a is a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16). Even with the same endpoint, different a give different curves (the larger a is, the more steeply it rises).
z-m-40-05.s.s3.prompt: Minjun said, “If the endpoints are the same, the two curves are the same curve.” Using the two formulas you made above as examples, answer Minjun, and write what more is needed besides the endpoint to determine the curve uniquely.
z-m-40-05.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute the same x (for example −1) into both formulas and compare y.
z-m-40-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which constant is determined if one more point that the curve passes through is given.
z-m-40-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show with numbers why the two formulas you gave have the same endpoint but are different curves?
z-m-40-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did it come across that the 'needed information' is information that fixes the value of a?
z-m-40-05.s.s3.model.0: No. Even though the endpoint is the same, (−2, 1), y = √(x+2)+1 and y = √(4x+8)+1 have values 2 and 3 at x = −1, so they are different curves. To determine the curve uniquely, besides the endpoint, we need one more point that the curve passes through.
z-m-40-05.s.s3.model.1: The endpoint alone is not enough. If a = 1, the curve is gentle, and if a = 9, it rises much more steeply, and both have the endpoint (−2, 1). We need information that tells the value of a, for example a point it passes through.
z-m-40-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: It did not use the specific value of a point, but it pointed out exactly the information that is needed.

z-m-40-06.title: What does it take for a correspondence joined from pieces to be one-to-one?
z-m-40-06.topic: The parameter condition for a piecewise function to be one-to-one, and the difference from a one-to-one correspondence
z-m-40-06.goal: Understand that a piecewise function is one-to-one only when the ranges of values made by the two pieces do not overlap, and distinguish one-to-one from a one-to-one correspondence (the range is the whole codomain) using the range of a.
z-m-40-06.material: There is the function f(x) = x + 2 (x < 1), f(x) = ax − 1 (x ≥ 1). (a is a constant. Read as: when x is less than 1, 'x plus 2'; when x is 1 or more, 'a x minus 1'.) “One-to-one” means that no two different x give the same function value, and a “one-to-one correspondence” is that and also the range equals the codomain (all real numbers). The domain and the codomain are both all real numbers.
z-m-40-06.thinking.0: Considering the range implied by the result of calculating one value
z-m-40-06.thinking.1: Finding several parameters that satisfy the condition
z-m-40-06.thinking.2: Distinguishing the conditions for one-to-one and one-to-one correspondence
z-m-40-06.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you have already learned the meaning of a function, the definitions of one-to-one functions and one-to-one correspondences, and calculating the values of piecewise functions.
z-m-40-06.prereq.1: Increasing and decreasing of the graph of a linear function (the sign of the slope)
z-m-40-06.prereq.2: Distinguishing the codomain from the range
z-m-40-06.s.s1.prompt: Minseo put a = 2 and calculated: f(−1) = 1, f(0) = 2, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 3. What can be said for certain from this calculation?
z-m-40-06.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a value other than a = 2 (for example 5), calculate f(−1) and f(1), and compare them.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the fact that it is not one-to-one for one a affects the result for other a.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.o.a: When a = 2 it is not one-to-one, and about other a we can't tell from this calculation alone
z-m-40-06.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that applies the result for one constant only to that constant.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.o.b: f(−1) = f(1) came out, so no matter what a we put in, f is not one-to-one
z-m-40-06.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that extends the result for one constant to all constants. Test what happens to f(−1) and f(1) for other a.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.o.c: f(2) = 3 is the largest value, so when a = 2, f is one-to-one
z-m-40-06.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that judges whether it is one-to-one from the fact that one large value came out. Look at whether there is a place where the same value came out twice.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.o.d: From this calculation alone we can't tell whether it is one-to-one for any a
z-m-40-06.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that misses even what the calculation tells us for certain about a = 2. Compare the values of f(−1) and f(1) again.
z-m-40-06.s.s1.explain: When a = 2, f(−1) = f(1) = 1, so it is certain that it is not one-to-one. Other a must be checked separately.
z-m-40-06.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different values of a for which f is one-to-one. (−10 ≤ a ≤ 10; decimals are allowed.)
z-m-40-06.s.s2.hint.0: Put in one value of a, and write down the range of values made by the left piece and the range of values made by the right piece.
z-m-40-06.s.s2.hint.1: See whether the two ranges overlap, and work out that for them not to overlap, the smallest value of the right piece must be at least how much.
z-m-40-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of the left piece and the values of the right piece do not overlap.
z-m-40-06.s.s2.fail.c2: For this a, there are different x1, x2 with f(x1) = f(x2). Find an x where the left formula (x < 1) and the right formula (x ≥ 1) give the same value.
z-m-40-06.s.s2.explain: The left piece (x < 1) gives every value less than 3. For the right piece (x ≥ 1) to be an increasing line, a > 0, and the ranges of the two do not overlap only if the minimum f(1) = a − 1 is 3 or more. That is, a ≥ 4. If a < 4, the same value comes out twice.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.prompt: This time we want to find a for which f is a one-to-one correspondence (the range is all real numbers). Which is right?
z-m-40-06.s.s3.hint.0: Shade on the number line the values that f can make when a = 5, and check whether any value is missing.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the cases a = 4 and a = 5, and look at whether the values connect near x = 1.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.r.a: This is thinking that if it is one-to-one then it is a one-to-one correspondence. Whether the range is all real numbers has to be examined separately.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.r.b: This is thinking that got confused about how to handle the value 3 at x = 1 at the boundary value a = 4. Compare the values that f makes when a = 4 and when a = 5.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.r.c: This is thinking that it is enough for the right piece just to be increasing. Check whether it overlaps with the values of the left piece.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.r.d: This is thinking that also considers the condition that for the range to be all real numbers, no value may be missing.
z-m-40-06.s.s3.explain: A one-to-one correspondence needs the range to be all real numbers, so no value can be missing. The left piece makes every value below 3, and the right piece makes every value of a − 1 or more. To not overlap and also have no gap between them, a − 1 = 3, that is, a = 4. If a > 4, the values between 3 and a − 1 are empty, so it is one-to-one but not a one-to-one correspondence.

z-m-40-07.title: If we raise the horizontal line, do the intersection points only increase?
z-m-40-07.topic: The graph of the quadratic with absolute value y=|x²−4| and how the number of intersections with a horizontal line changes
z-m-40-07.goal: As the height k of the horizontal line changes, explain why the number of intersections does not just increase but changes as 0, 2, 4, 3, 2, connecting it to the shape of the graph (the folded peak and the points touching the x-axis).
z-m-40-07.material: The number of points where the graph of the function y = |x² − 4| (read as: 'the absolute value of x squared minus 4') meets the horizontal line y = k is equal to the number of different real roots of the equation |x² − 4| = k. Below are the values of y calculated at some values of x. When x is −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, y is 5, 0, 3, 4, 3, 0, 5.
z-m-40-07.thinking.0: Making a prediction, checking it by calculation, and revising it
z-m-40-07.thinking.1: Finding the k values that serve as boundaries
z-m-40-07.thinking.2: Connecting the shape of the graph with the number of roots
z-m-40-07.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the graph of a quadratic function, the meaning of absolute value, and the interpretation that the real roots of an equation are the intersection points of the graph and a horizontal line.
z-m-40-07.prereq.1: Solutions of the quadratic equation x² = m (two if m > 0, one if m = 0, none if m < 0)
z-m-40-07.prereq.2: The absolute value |t| is t if t ≥ 0 and −t if t < 0
z-m-40-07.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed as k changes. Each time, choose the number of intersection points.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.hint.0: Follow the values in the table, and count the number of times the graph passes the place where y = k, one interval at a time.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.hint.1: Split into the two equations x² − 4 = k and x² − 4 = −k, and work out how many x come out of each.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.info: First, draw the horizontal line y = 1, with k = 1.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many different points does the horizontal line y = 1 share with the graph?
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.after: |x² − 4| = 1 means x² − 4 = 1 or x² − 4 = −1, so x² = 5 or x² = 3. x = ±√5, ±√3, which is 4 points. In the table, the values go down from x = 1 (y = 3) to x = 2 (y = 0), and go up from x = 2 to x = 3 (y = 5), so on the right side it crosses y = 1 twice, and the left side is the same.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is thinking that it meets only as one pair, left and right, like a parabola.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is thinking that, following the shape of the table values going down and then up, it crosses twice on each of the left and right sides.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is thinking that, because of the shape touching the x-axis, one more point is added.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is thinking that, since there is no x with y = 1 in the table, they do not meet. Think about the values between the entries of the table.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.info: This time, draw the horizontal line y = 4, with k = 4. In the table, y = 4 when x = 0.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many different points does the horizontal line y = 4 share with the graph?
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.after: From x² − 4 = 4, x = ±2√2 (2 points), and from x² − 4 = −4, x = 0 (1 point), and they do not coincide, so there are 3 in all. k = 4 is the height of the peak of the part folded upward at x = 0, so the horizontal line just grazes the peak.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is thinking that the number is the same even if k changes.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is thinking that misses touching once at x = 0 and counts only the two outer points.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is thinking that counts together the one touching point at x = 0 and the two outer points.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is thinking that, because k became larger, the intersections also increase.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.info: Finally, draw the horizontal line y = 5, with k = 5.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many different points does the horizontal line y = 5 share with the graph?
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.after: From x² − 4 = 5, x = ±3 (2 points), and x² − 4 = −5 means x² = −1, which has no real roots. There are 2 in all. When k becomes greater than 4, the horizontal line rises above the folded peak, and only the two outer branches remain.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is thinking that the higher you raise k, the more intersections there are.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is thinking that carries over the number from when k = 4.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is thinking that, since it went beyond the peak height 4, they no longer meet. Check whether there is an x with y = 5 in the table.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is thinking that once it rises above the folded peak, it meets only the two outer places.
z-m-40-07.s.s1.reflect: Did you think the intersections only increase as k is raised? Explain why, when k is raised from a very small value, the number of intersections changes as 0 → 2 → 4 → 3 → 2, connecting it to the points of the graph touching the x-axis and to the folded peak.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.prompt: As k is raised slowly from a very small negative number, write all the boundary values of k where the number of intersections changes, and explain which part of the graph the horizontal line passes through at each boundary.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.hint.0: In the table, find what part of the graph the point on the x-axis (y = 0) and the point at x = 0 (y = 4) are.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.hint.1: Set k just below and just above a boundary, and compare the numbers of intersections.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: The boundaries are k = ... and ...
z-m-40-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why the boundary k values are those values, and the height of which point on the graph they are?
z-m-40-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Around each boundary (when k is less than the boundary and when it is greater), did you say how many intersections there are?
z-m-40-07.s.s2.model.0: The boundaries are k=0 and k=4. k=0 is the height of x=±2, where the horizontal line touches the x-axis, and when it goes above that, there are 4 intersections. k=4 is the height of the peak folded at x=0, so there are 3 then, and when it becomes greater than 4, only 2 remain.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.model.1: When you raise the horizontal line, it first touches the graph at k=0 (2 intersections), between 0 and 4 there are 4, at k=4 it passes the peak at x=0 and there are 3, and when k is greater than 4 it meets only the two outer places, so there are 2. So the values that make the change are 0 and 4.
z-m-40-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: This is an answer that also includes the case of 0 points when k < 0.

z-m-40-08.title: If we know only that f(1) = f(5), is the quadratic function unique?
z-m-40-08.topic: Symmetry of quadratic functions: what f(1)=f(5) tells us and the freedom that remains
z-m-40-08.goal: Understand that two points with the same function value fix only the axis of symmetry of a quadratic function and not the function, confirm that it may still not be determined uniquely even with more conditions, and distinguish conditions that give new information from those that do not.
z-m-40-08.material: For the quadratic function f(x) = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0), only the fact f(1) = f(5) is known. (Read as: 'f of 1 and f of 5 are equal'.) Seonwoo said, “There are two points with the same value, so f is determined uniquely.”
z-m-40-08.thinking.0: Telling apart what is settled by the given information and what is not
z-m-40-08.thinking.1: Building several functions that satisfy the condition
z-m-40-08.thinking.2: Telling apart new information from information that is already included
z-m-40-08.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the left-right symmetry of the graph of a quadratic function and the formula in the form f(x) = a(x − p)² + q.
z-m-40-08.prereq.2: The fact that two points at the same height are at the same distance from the axis of symmetry
z-m-40-08.s.s1.prompt: What can be said for certain from the fact f(1) = f(5)?
z-m-40-08.s.s1.hint.0: Build two quadratic functions that satisfy f(1) = f(5) yourself, and check by substituting values.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.hint.1: On the graphs of the two functions you made, write separately what is the same and what is different.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.o.a: We can know the y-coordinate of the vertex of the graph
z-m-40-08.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that treats knowing the axis of symmetry and knowing the height of the vertex as the same thing. Build functions with different heights.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that mixes up and takes the value at the middle x of the two points as 0. The middle is the axis of symmetry, not a root.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.o.c: The axis of symmetry of the graph is x = 3
z-m-40-08.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that reads the axis of symmetry from the positions of the two points with the same value.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.o.d: We can know the value of a
z-m-40-08.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that symmetry alone also fixes the width of the graph. Build a function with a different a yourself.
z-m-40-08.s.s1.explain: The graph of a quadratic function is symmetric left and right about the axis of symmetry, so the x-coordinates of two points with the same value are at the same distance from the axis. So the axis is x = 3, exactly in the middle of the two x. But we cannot know the height of the vertex or the width a.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.prompt: We also learned that f(0) = 5. Writing f(x) = a(x − 3)² + q, find 3 different integer pairs (a, q) that satisfy both f(1) = f(5) and f(0) = 5 and have a minimum (a > 0). (a ≤ 5)
z-m-40-08.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate f(0) = a(0 − 3)² + q and first write the relation between a and q.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.hint.1: Put values like 1, 2, 3 in for a to find q, and check that you keep the conditions a ≤ 5 and a > 0.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a is a positive integer 5 or less, and q is an integer.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be a positive integer 5 or less, and q must be an integer.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Adjust a and q so that f(0) = a(0 − 3)² + q = 5.
z-m-40-08.s.s2.explain: f(0) = 9a + q = 5, so q = 5 − 9a. Each time you change a, a different function comes out (if a = 1 then q = −4, if a = 2 then q = −13, ...). Even knowing the axis of symmetry and one point, it is still not determined uniquely.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.prompt: In addition to f(1) = f(5) and f(0) = 5 known so far, choose all the information that helps determine f uniquely.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.hint.0: Put each piece of information into f(x) = a(x − 3)² + q and write whether a new equation in a and q arises.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the new equation is different from the equation that came from f(0) = 5 or is the same equation.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.r.a: This is thinking that if you know the height of the vertex, the relation between a and q fixes things uniquely.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.r.b: This is thinking that misses that 6 is symmetric to 0 and takes it as new information.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.r.c: This is thinking that the value at a new point away from the axis gives one more relation.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.r.d: This is thinking that takes a repetition, in other words, of symmetry that is already known as new information.
z-m-40-08.s.s3.explain: The axis of symmetry is x = 3, so f(6) = f(0) and f(2) = f(4) are facts that already hold, so they are not new information. The minimum value −4 gives q = −4 and so a = 1, and f(4) = −3 gives a + q = −3, which together with 9a + q = 5 fixes a = 1 and q = −4.

z-m-40-09.title: With two villages and with three villages, where should the bus stop go?
z-m-40-09.topic: Sum of absolute value functions: the broken-line graph of the sum of distances S(x) and where it is smallest
z-m-40-09.goal: Understand that the sum of distances to two villages has a flat bottom, so the position of the minimum is many places, confirm that with three villages the position of the minimum is fixed to one place, and predict for yourself the case of four villages.
z-m-40-09.material: On a straight road, positions are expressed as x km. Village A is at x = 2 and village B is at x = 6. We want to build one bus stop at position x on the road. If the sum of the distances from the stop to each village is S(x), then S(x) = |x − 2| + |x − 6|. (Read as: 'the absolute value of x minus 2, plus the absolute value of x minus 6'.) The stop can be built anywhere on the road.
z-m-40-09.thinking.0: Predicting by intuition where the minimum is, and checking by calculation
z-m-40-09.thinking.1: Finding several positions that satisfy a condition
z-m-40-09.thinking.2: Predicting the rule when the number of villages changes
z-m-40-09.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the interpretation that the absolute value |x − p| is the distance between x and p on the number line.
z-m-40-09.prereq.1: Calculating the value of a linear expression with absolute value
z-m-40-09.prereq.2: Positions and distances on the number line
z-m-40-09.s.s1.prompt: Where is the position x of the stop at which S(x) is smallest?
z-m-40-09.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate S(x) at x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and write them in a table.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.hint.1: Look at how many x give the smallest value of S, and in what range those x are.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that between the two villages the sum of the distances is constant.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that the single point in the middle of the two villages is best.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.o.c: x = 2 or x = 6, that is, only right on a village
z-m-40-09.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that it is closest if it is built right on a village.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that only near the middle is good.
z-m-40-09.s.s1.explain: If x is between 2 and 6, S(x) = (x − 2) + (6 − x) = 4, which is constant. If it goes outside, it increases. So the graph of S(x) has a flat bottom for 2 ≤ x ≤ 6.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.prompt: Village C (x = 10) has appeared. Now S₃(x) = |x − 2| + |x − 6| + |x − 10|. Find 3 different integer positions x of the stop for which the sum of distances to the three villages is 10 or less. (−5 ≤ x ≤ 15)
z-m-40-09.s.s2.hint.0: Put one value in for x, find the three distances separately, and add them.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.hint.1: Change the values and narrow down where the boundaries are, on the side where the sum becomes greater than 10 (left and right).
z-m-40-09.s.s2.ok.c1: x is an integer from −5 to 15.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be an integer from −5 to 15.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the distances to the three villages is 10 or less.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the distances to the three villages is greater than 10. Find the three distances separately and add them again.
z-m-40-09.s.s2.explain: The minimum of S₃(x) is 8 at the middle village x = 6, and it increases as you go to either side. The values 10 or less are 4 ≤ x ≤ 8. Unlike the case of two villages, there is no flat bottom, and the position of the minimum is the single place 6.
z-m-40-09.s.s3.prompt: Explain how the position where the sum of distances is smallest differs between 2 villages (2, 6) and 3 villages (2, 6, 10), and write your prediction of what happens with 4 villages (2, 6, 10, 14).
z-m-40-09.s.s3.hint.0: With 4 villages, calculate S₄(x) at x = 6, 8, 10 and compare.
z-m-40-09.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many middle villages there were with 2 villages and with 3 villages.
z-m-40-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: With 2 villages, ..., and with 3 villages, ..., so with 4 villages ...
z-m-40-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your own words the difference between an even number of villages and an odd number of villages?
z-m-40-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test your prediction for 4 villages with a calculation (for example S₄ at x = 8)?
z-m-40-09.s.s3.model.0: With 2 villages, anywhere between 2 and 6 the sum is the same, 4, so the position of the minimum is many places (an interval). With 3 villages, only at the middle village 6 is the sum smallest, 8, so it is fixed to one place. With 4 villages, I think everything between the middle two villages 6 and 10 will be the minimum (sum 16).
z-m-40-09.s.s3.model.1: With 2 villages (2, 6) there is a flat bottom, so anywhere from 2 to 6 works, and with 3 villages (2, 6, 10) the middle village 6 is the only minimum. With 4 villages (2, 6, 10, 14), I predict that the whole interval between the middle two villages will be the minimum again.

z-m-40-10.title: If the values in a table are equal on the left and right, is the graph symmetric too?
z-m-40-10.topic: Symmetry of a function graph about the y-axis: the strength of evidence that a few pairs of values are equal, and building counterexamples
z-m-40-10.goal: Based on the definition of symmetry about the y-axis (f(−x) = f(x) for all x), understand that a table showing a few pairs of values are equal cannot settle symmetry, and build a counterexample yourself from a function that fits the table exactly but is not symmetric.
z-m-40-10.material: The formula of the function f is not known, and there is a table with values at only a few x. When x is −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, f(x) is 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. The values at x not in the table are not known. The domain is all real numbers, and “symmetric about the y-axis” means that f(−x) = f(x) holds for all real numbers x. Jiho said, “In the table the values at x and −x are equal, so the graph of f is symmetric about the y-axis.”
z-m-40-10.thinking.0: Considering how far finite evidence reaches
z-m-40-10.thinking.1: Telling apart the grounds that settle “for all x”
z-m-40-10.thinking.2: Building a counterexample that fits the table
z-m-40-10.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the meaning of symmetry about the y-axis (if the point (x, y) exists, then (−x, y) exists too) and how to calculate the values of polynomials.
z-m-40-10.prereq.1: Substituting values into the polynomial x(x² − 1)(x² − 4) and calculating
z-m-40-10.prereq.2: The sense that replacing x with −x changes the sign of terms of odd degree
z-m-40-10.s.s1.hint.0: Separate the x that are in the table from those that are not, and look at whether f(−x) and f(x) can be compared for each.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how far the phrase “for all real numbers x” reaches in the table.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.o.a: At x = ±1, ±2, f(−x) = f(x), and we don't know about the rest
z-m-40-10.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that distinguishes the pairs that were checked from the values that were not checked.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.o.b: Both pairs checked in the table are right, so it has been confirmed that the graph is symmetric about the y-axis
z-m-40-10.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that stretches a few checked pairs to all x. “For all x” includes x not in the table.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.o.c: There are only two pairs, so nothing can be said with this table
z-m-40-10.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that throws away even the fact that it holds for the two pairs that were checked. Read again what the table actually shows.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.o.d: Both pairs were right, so it is likely symmetric and is practically proven
z-m-40-10.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that treats an increasing number of checked pairs as the same as proof. A finite number of checks cannot rule out a counterexample.
z-m-40-10.s.s1.explain: The table shows that f(−x) = f(x) only at x = ±1, ±2. At x not in the table it is not known, so we cannot confirm that it is symmetric about the y-axis.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.prompt: What kind of grounds are needed to confirm that the graph is symmetric about the y-axis?
z-m-40-10.s.s2.hint.0: Compare whether one x is enough for a counterexample showing it is not symmetric, and how many x are enough to confirm that it is symmetric.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the number of grounds needed when proving “for all” and when disproving it.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.o.a: If we also write the values at x = ±3, ±4, ±5 in the table and they are all the same, symmetry is confirmed
z-m-40-10.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that if you add more points, the whole is confirmed. Even if you check a finite number more, a counterexample can remain outside the table.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.o.b: If you plot many points and connect them, it takes a shape that looks roughly equal on the left and right
z-m-40-10.s.s2.r.b: This is thinking that uses the impression seen by eye as grounds. Slightly different values do not show in a picture.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.o.c: When a formula is given, calculate f(−x) and show that it is the same expression as f(x)
z-m-40-10.s.s2.r.c: This is thinking that shows it holds for the letter x, handling “all x” at once.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.o.d: If the proportion of pairs in the table that match is half or more, symmetry is confirmed
z-m-40-10.s.s2.r.d: This is thinking that judges “for all x” by a proportion criterion. If even one fails, it is not symmetric.
z-m-40-10.s.s2.explain: To confirm “f(−x) = f(x) for all x,” you must show it with a formula in the letter x or deal with all x in some other way. Checking more points in the table can increase belief, but it does not confirm.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.prompt: The functions g(x) = x² + c·x(x² − 1)(x² − 4) (c is a constant) satisfy the values of the table exactly at x = 0, ±1, ±2 (0; 1, 1; 4, 4) (check by substituting the values yourself). Build evidence that some of these functions are not symmetric: choose a nonzero integer c (−3 ≤ c ≤ 3) and a positive number t so that g(t) ≠ g(−t), and find 2 different (c, t).
z-m-40-10.s.s3.hint.0: Fix one c and t, calculate g(t) and g(−t) separately, and compare.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what happens when you put in t as a value in the table (1, 2) and as a value not in the table (such as 3).
z-m-40-10.s.s3.ok.c1: c is a nonzero integer from −3 to 3.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.fail.c1: c must be a nonzero integer from −3 to 3.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.fail.c2: t must be a positive number.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.ok.c3: g(t) and g(−t) are different. This is evidence that it is not symmetric about the y-axis.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.fail.c3: For this t, g(t) and g(−t) are the same. It is a value in the table or a value where they come out equal. Test another t.
z-m-40-10.s.s3.explain: x(x² − 1)(x² − 4) is 0 at x = 0, ±1, ±2, so the values of the table stay the same, but when x is replaced by −x, the sign becomes opposite. So if t is not 1 or 2, g(t) and g(−t) differ by twice c·t(t² − 1)(t² − 4). This is a counterexample showing that the five values of the table alone cannot confirm symmetry.

z-m-40-11.title: Reading the signs of the coefficients from a graph shape heard in words: which line is first wrong?
z-m-40-11.topic: The shape of the graph of the quadratic y=ax²+bx+c and the signs of the coefficients
z-m-40-11.goal: Find the first line that goes wrong in a solution that organized the signs of and relations among a, b, c from four features of a graph, confirm why it is wrong by testing with specific numbers, and build an (a, b, c) that satisfies all four conditions yourself.
z-m-40-11.material: We describe the graph of the quadratic function y = ax² + bx + c only in words. ① It opens downward (∩ shape). ② The vertex is to the right of the y-axis (the x-coordinate of the vertex is positive). ③ The point where it meets the y-axis is below the x-axis (its y-coordinate is negative). ④ It meets the x-axis at two different points. a, b, c are real constants. Below is Hyunwoo's solution, in which he decided the signs of a, b, c from this description.
z-m-40-11.thinking.0: Finding the error line by line in a solution
z-m-40-11.thinking.1: Testing a judgment with specific values
z-m-40-11.thinking.2: Building an example that satisfies several conditions at the same time
z-m-40-11.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you have already learned that in y = ax² + bx + c, c is the y-intercept, the x-coordinate of the vertex is −b/(2a), and the discriminant is related to the number of intersections with the x-axis.
z-m-40-11.prereq.1: Calculating the signs of inequalities and fractions (the sign of a quotient when the denominator is negative)
z-m-40-11.prereq.2: The direction in which a quadratic function opens and the sign of a
z-m-40-11.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Hyunwoo's solution that goes wrong.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.hint.0: Separate out the sign judgment of each line, and check whether it is right by putting in specific numbers (for example a = −1).
z-m-40-11.s.s1.hint.1: In line 3, test with numbers what the sign of the numerator must be for the quotient to be positive when the denominator is negative.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.line.0: ① It opens downward, so a < 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.line.1: ③ The y-coordinate of the point where it meets the y-axis is the value c at x = 0, so c < 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.line.2: ② The x-coordinate of the vertex, −b/(2a), is positive and a < 0, so the numerator −b must also be positive. Therefore b < 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.line.3: ④ It meets at two different points, so b² − 4ac > 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. If −b/(2a) is positive and the denominator 2a is negative, then for the quotient to be positive the numerator −b must be negative. So b > 0. Line 5 carries over this mistake. Lines 1, 2, 4 are correct.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.prompt: What is the quickest test to show whether the signs Hyunwoo decided (a < 0, b < 0, c < 0) fit the description?
z-m-40-11.s.s2.hint.0: Choose specific numbers that fit Hyunwoo's signs and complete the formula y = ax² + bx + c.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.hint.1: With that formula, check descriptions ① to ④ one by one.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.o.a: Calculate the position of the vertex with a = −1, b = −4, c = −3
z-m-40-11.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that turns the result of the judgment into specific values and checks it against the conditions of the description.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.o.b: Recalculate and check whether b² − 4ac > 0 holds
z-m-40-11.s.s2.r.b: This is thinking that rechecks a line that was written correctly. The 4th line is not wrong in this solution.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.o.c: Since c < 0, recheck whether the graph meets the y-axis below the x-axis
z-m-40-11.s.s2.r.c: This is thinking that rechecks a line that was written correctly. The 2nd line is not wrong in this solution.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.o.d: Assume that if a < 0 then y < 0 for all x, and draw the graph
z-m-40-11.s.s2.r.d: This is thinking that if it opens downward, all values are negative. The vertex can also be above the x-axis.
z-m-40-11.s.s2.explain: If (a, b, c) = (−1, −4, −3), then y = −x² − 4x − 3 and the x-coordinate of the vertex is −b/(2a) = −2, which is negative. It does not match description ② (the vertex is to the right of the y-axis), so b < 0 is wrong.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.prompt: Find 3 different integer triples (a, b, c) that satisfy all of descriptions ① to ④. (a ≠ 0 and −6 ≤ a, b, c ≤ 6)
z-m-40-11.s.s3.hint.0: Organize separately which of the signs of, or relations among, a, b, c each of ① to ④ is talking about.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.hint.1: Fix one candidate, substitute ① to ④ one by one, and see which condition it gets stuck on, then fix it.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, c are integers from −6 to 6 and a ≠ 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.fail.c1: a, b, c are integers from −6 to 6, and a must not be 0.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.fail.c2: ①: It does not open downward.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.ok.c3: ② The x-coordinate of the vertex is positive.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.fail.c3: ②: The vertex is not to the right of the y-axis.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.ok.c4: ③ The point where it meets the y-axis is below the x-axis.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.fail.c4: ③: The point where it meets the y-axis is not below the x-axis.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.ok.c5: ④ It meets the x-axis at two different points.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.fail.c5: ④: It does not meet the x-axis at two different points.
z-m-40-11.s.s3.explain: ①→a < 0, ③→c < 0, ②→the signs of a and b are opposite (so b > 0), ④→b² > 4ac. For example, y = −x² + 4x − 3 meets the x-axis at x = 1, 3 and its vertex is (2, 1).

z-m-40-12.title: The message “1/x is a decreasing function”: is it okay to send it as it is?
z-m-40-12.topic: Increasing and decreasing of the inverse proportion function y=1/x: speaking by dividing into intervals
z-m-40-12.goal: Show with a counterexample that y = 1/x is decreasing on the positive side and on the negative side separately, but cannot be said to be decreasing on all x ≠ 0, and rewrite the message to send to a junior student by dividing into intervals.
z-m-40-12.material: A senior student wants to send the message below to a junior student about the function y = 1/x (x ≠ 0). (Read as: 'y is 1 over x'.) “Decreasing” means that if x1 < x2, then always f(x1) > f(x2).
z-m-40-12.thinking.0: Finding the overgeneralization in the message
z-m-40-12.thinking.2: Rewriting it to suit the person receiving it
z-m-40-12.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the definition of increasing and decreasing functions (it is decreasing if f(x1) > f(x2) when x1 < x2) and how to calculate the value of the fraction 1/x.
z-m-40-12.prereq.1: The calculation that the reciprocal of a negative number is negative
z-m-40-12.prereq.2: The meaning of intervals (the positive side, the negative side)
z-m-40-12.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in the senior student's message that goes wrong.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.hint.0: Write which x are being compared with each other in each line.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.hint.1: Find x1, x2 that break the “always” in line 3, and substitute them yourself.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.line.0: For y = 1/x, when x = 1, 2, 4, y = 1, 1/2, 1/4, so as x gets larger, y gets smaller.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.line.1: Also when x = −4, −2, −1, y = −1/4, −1/2, −1, so as x gets larger, y gets smaller.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.line.2: So if x1 < x2, then always 1/x1 > 1/x2, and this function is decreasing on all real numbers with x ≠ 0.
z-m-40-12.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. Lines 1 and 2 compare positives with positives and negatives with negatives, so they are correct. But if x1 = −1 and x2 = 1, then 1/x1 = −1 < 1 = 1/x2, so x got larger and y also got larger. Comparisons that cross between the positive side and the negative side were not checked.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.prompt: Build counterexamples showing that the “always” in line 3 is wrong. Find 3 different pairs (x1, x2) with x1 < x2 and 1/x1 < 1/x2. x1 and x2 are nonzero numbers.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.hint.0: Change the signs of x1 and x2, and compare the signs and sizes of 1/x1 and 1/x2.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.hint.1: When you make the three pairs, look at whether the results all have the same combination of signs.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.fail.c1: x1 and x2 must not be 0.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.fail.c2: x1 must be less than x2.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.ok.c3: x got larger and 1/x also got larger. This is a counterexample.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.fail.c3: In this pair, when x gets larger, 1/x gets smaller or stays the same. It is not a counterexample.
z-m-40-12.s.s2.explain: For 1/x1 < 1/x2, x1 must be negative and x2 must be positive (x1 < 0 < x2). When it is negative, 1/x is negative, and when it is positive, it is positive, so where the sign changes, the value of y jumps up.
z-m-40-12.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the message to send again to the junior student in one or two sentences. Also include on what range it can be said to be decreasing.
z-m-40-12.s.s3.hint.0: Divide into the positive side and the negative side, and write one sentence for each about what happens to y when x gets larger.
z-m-40-12.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one of the counterexample pairs you just made and put it in the message.
z-m-40-12.s.s3.placeholder: Example: y = 1/x, on ... and on ... separately, ...
z-m-40-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: So the junior student does not misunderstand it as “always decreasing,” did you write together how far it is right and where it breaks?
z-m-40-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate and check that the numerical example you gave is really a case where x gets larger and y also gets larger?
z-m-40-12.s.s3.model.0: y=1/x is decreasing on the interval x>0 and on the interval x<0 separately, but we can't say it is decreasing on the whole. When x=−1, y=−1, and when x=1, y=1, so x got larger and y also got larger.
z-m-40-12.s.s3.model.1: If you compare positives with positives and negatives with negatives, y gets smaller when x gets larger, so it is a decreasing function on each interval. But going from −2 to 3, y increases from −1/2 to 1/3, so we must not write that it is decreasing on all x≠0.

z-m-40-13.title: Can we state the solution of an inequality from just two intersection points?
z-m-40-13.topic: The positional relation of a quadratic function and a line: the solution of the inequality f(x) > g(x) when only the x-coordinates of the two intersection points are known
z-m-40-13.goal: Understand that the x-coordinates of the two intersection points alone do not decide which graph is above, so the solution of the inequality splits into two possibilities, confirm how information about one point changes the judgment, and build a quadratic function and line for the opposite case yourself.
z-m-40-13.material: The graph (parabola) of the quadratic function y = f(x) and the line y = g(x) meet at two points, x = 1 and x = 5. That is, f(1) = g(1) and f(5) = g(5). We want to know the solution of the inequality f(x) > g(x). Sua said, “The solution is between the two intersection points.” It is not yet known whether the parabola opens downward or upward.
z-m-40-13.thinking.0: Saying what additional information is needed
z-m-40-13.thinking.1: Evaluating whether new information strengthens the grounds for a judgment
z-m-40-13.prereq.0: The assigned level H3 is only a difficulty level in this production distribution, and it does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade. Assumption: you already know the idea of the intersection points of a quadratic function and a line, and that the sign of a quadratic expression differs between the two roots and outside them.
z-m-40-13.prereq.1: Comparing function values, and the idea of seeing the function f(x) − g(x) as a new function
z-m-40-13.prereq.2: The direction in which a quadratic function opens (downward, upward)
z-m-40-13.s.s1.prompt: When only the x-coordinates of the intersection points, 1 and 5, are known, what can be said about the solution of the inequality f(x) > g(x)?
z-m-40-13.s.s1.hint.0: Draw by yourself whether there are pictures that look different from each other but have the same two intersection points.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.hint.1: Draw the graph of f for when it opens downward and when it opens upward, and compare which one is above between the two intersection points.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.o.a: The solution is determined to be between the two intersection points, 1 < x < 5
z-m-40-13.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that between the intersection points is always the solution. Draw what happens if the parabola bends the other way.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.o.b: The solution is determined to be outside the intersection points, x < 1 or x > 5
z-m-40-13.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that outside the intersection points is always the solution. Draw what happens if the parabola bends the other way.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.o.c: Both cases are possible, so more information about which is above is needed
z-m-40-13.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that the positions of the intersection points alone do not decide which is above.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.o.d: We can't tell: because we need to know the y-coordinates of the two intersection points too
z-m-40-13.s.s1.r.d: This is thinking that y-coordinates are necessary even though the x-coordinates are enough information. Work out what is needed to decide which is above.
z-m-40-13.s.s1.explain: f(x) − g(x) is a quadratic expression and is 0 at x = 1, 5, so it has the form p(x − 1)(x − 5) (p ≠ 0). If p < 0, the solution is 1 < x < 5, and if p > 0, it is x < 1 or x > 5. The sign of p cannot be known from the intersection points alone.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.prompt: New information came in: at x = 3, f(3) = 7 and g(3) = 3. How can we now view Sua's claim “1 < x < 5”?
z-m-40-13.s.s2.hint.0: See f(x) − g(x) as a new function, and first check whether its value at x = 3 is positive or negative.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether the sign of a quadratic expression can change between the two roots, and where it would have to pass through for it to change.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.o.a: The sign changes only at 1 and 5, and at x = 3 f is above, so between them is the solution
z-m-40-13.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that knows why the sign at one point carries over to the whole interval.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.o.b: We still can't tell. One point can't be the ground for the whole interval
z-m-40-13.s.s2.r.b: This is thinking that misses that the information at one point carries over to the whole interval. Work out whether the sign can change between the two intersection points.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.o.c: x < 1 or x > 5 is the solution. The farther from the intersection points, the more f is above
z-m-40-13.s.s2.r.c: This is thinking that decides the direction without grounds. Read the value at x = 3 again.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.o.d: It holds only at x = 3, and we can't tell at other x
z-m-40-13.s.s2.r.d: This is thinking that misses that the value changes continuously, so it must pass through 0 for the sign to change.
z-m-40-13.s.s2.explain: f(x) − g(x) is a quadratic expression, so the only places where the sign changes are the roots x = 1, 5. At x = 3 between the two roots, if f − g = 4 > 0, then it is positive on the whole between them and negative outside. So Sua's conclusion now has grounds. At first, it was in a state where the conclusion might or might not be right.
z-m-40-13.s.s3.prompt: This time, build a case where Sua's conclusion is wrong. Let f(x) = px² + qx + r (p ≠ 0) and g(x) = mx + n, and find 2 different (p, q, r, m, n) such that the two graphs meet at x = 1 and x = 5 and f(3) < g(3).
z-m-40-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write the conditions of the two intersection points as the equations f(1) = g(1) and f(5) = g(5).
z-m-40-13.s.s3.hint.1: Fix some of p, q, r first, and then adjust m and n so that g passes through the two points (1, f(1)) and (5, f(5)).
z-m-40-13.s.s3.fail.c1: f must be a quadratic function (p ≠ 0).
z-m-40-13.s.s3.ok.c2: The two graphs meet at x = 1.
z-m-40-13.s.s3.fail.c2: At x = 1, f(1) and g(1) are different.
z-m-40-13.s.s3.ok.c3: The two graphs meet at x = 5.
z-m-40-13.s.s3.fail.c3: At x = 5, f(5) and g(5) are different.
z-m-40-13.s.s3.fail.c4: At x = 3, f(3) is not less than g(3).
z-m-40-13.s.s3.explain: Since f(x) − g(x) = p(x − 1)(x − 5), f(3) − g(3) = −4p. So if p > 0, f(3) < g(3), and f > g where x < 1 or x > 5. If p < 0, between them is the solution. Even with the same positions of the intersection points, the solution differs depending on the direction the parabola opens.
